query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor co-addition of rhenium (Re) and boron (B) to equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW, followed by a segregation heat treatment that drives B to grain boundaries (GBs) while retaining a single-phase BCC matrix, will increase room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance without degrading high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW polycrystal (coarse to medium grain size), homogenized to remove casting segregation.
generation.intervention: Alloy to (NbMoTaW)97.8Re2.0B0.2 (at.%), solutionize at 1400–1500 °C to maintain single-phase BCC, then age at 800–950 °C for 2–24 h to promote B grain-boundary segregation without forming borides or ordered intermetallics.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests: room temperature and up to 1600 °C in inert atmosphere. Irradiation: He implantation (10–100 keV) to 1e17–1e18 He/m^2 at 300–800 °C; heavy-ion (e.g., Kr/Fe) to 1–10 dpa at 300–800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometer-scale B enrichment films (≈0.5–1 nm) at GBs that raise GB cohesive energy, and dilute Re enrichment around dislocation cores/short-range order within the BCC matrix that lowers screw-dislocation Peierls stress; both together increase sink strength for point defects at GBs without forming second phases.
generation.mechanism: Re locally modifies the electronic structure and dislocation core character in the BCC matrix, lowering the Peierls barrier for screw dislocation glide and enabling more homogeneous plasticity at room temperature. Segregated B strengthens GB cohesion, shifting fracture from intergranular to transgranular and delaying crack initiation. Under irradiation, B-decorated GBs and Re-modified matrix act as efficient sinks for vacancies and interstitials and as traps for small He clusters, delaying bubble coarsening and surface blistering; mass and bonding disorder further frustrate irradiation-enhanced ordering/precipitation, preserving the single-phase BCC state.
generation.predicted_outcome:
- Room-temperature tensile ductility: absolute elongation increases from near-zero (<1%) to approximately 3–6%; work-hardening becomes measurable (non-zero n). Yield strength at RT changes by less than ±10% relative to baseline.
- High-temperature strength (e.g., 1600 °C compression/tension): retained within ±10% of baseline NbMoTaW; creep rate at given stress within a factor of 1.2 of baseline.
- Irradiation tolerance: after 30–100 keV He implantation to 1e18 He/m^2 at 500 °C, near-surface He bubble density and average bubble size reduced by roughly 30–50%, and onset fluence for blistering increases by at least 2× compared to baseline. After 5–10 dpa heavy-ion irradiation at 600 °C, irradiation hardening reduced by ~20–40% and no irradiation-induced amorphization or second-phase precipitation detectable by TEM/APT.
- Phase stability: single-phase BCC retained after thermal exposure at 1100 °C for 100 h.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic NbMoTaW (single-phase BCC) with excellent high-temperature strength (up to ~1600 °C), poor room-temperature ductility (near-zero elongation), and unestablished experimental irradiation response.
generation.boundary:
- Composition: Re ≤ 3 at.% and B = 0.1–0.3 at.% to avoid sigma/chi/Laves or boride precipitation; higher B (>0.5 at.%) or Re (>4–5 at.%) risks embrittlement and second phases.
- Temperature: benefits to ductility are most evident at 20–300 °C; above ~1200 °C, B segregation may partially dissolve, reducing GB cohesion benefit (mechanical properties should remain comparable to baseline). 
- Irradiation: improvements expected for 10–100 keV He and 1–10 dpa at 300–800 °C; at very low T (<100 °C) defect mobility is too low for GB sinks to be effective; at very high He energies (>200 keV) or very high doses (>10 dpa), bubble coarsening and radiation-induced precipitation risks may overcome benefits.
- Microstructure: requires single-phase BCC matrix and clean GBs; significant oxygen contamination or pre-existing carbides/borides at GBs will negate the GB cohesion mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative gains are estimates; the exact magnitude of ductility increase and irradiation tolerance depends on achieved B segregation level, Re distribution, grain size, and impurity content. There is risk of irradiation-enhanced precipitation (e.g., sigma/Laves) if local Re/Mo/W partitioning occurs, and risk of boride formation if B exceeds the segregation capacity or if processing pushes GBs out of equilibrium. Trade-offs between defect recombination (beneficial) and reduced diffusion (from Re) are not fully predictable a priori.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare NbMoTaW and (NbMoTaW)97.8Re2.0B0.2 ingots; identical melt/thermomechanical history; solutionize at 1450 °C, then age at 900 °C (optimize 2–24 h). Confirm single-phase BCC and quantify B GB segregation (APT/EELS). Test (i) RT uniaxial tension on dogbones; (ii) 1600 °C compression (or tension) at matched strain rate; (iii) He implantation at 30 keV to 1e18 He/m^2 at 500 °C and heavy-ion irradiation to 5 dpa at 600 °C. Characterize irradiated layers by cross-sectional TEM (bubble size/density), APT (segregation/precipitates), nanoindentation (hardening), and SEM (blistering area).
measurements: RT tensile elongation to failure and yield/UTS for both alloys
High-temperature (1600 °C) yield/flow strength or creep rate at fixed stress
He bubble size distribution and number density at fixed fluence/temperature
Surface blistered area fraction and blister size distribution
Irradiation-induced hardness change (nanoindentation) at matched dpa
Phase stability: XRD/TEM/APT for any ordered/second phases post-irradiation and post-aging
Grain-boundary B areal density and width (APT/EELS line scans)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following hold under the specified conditions: (1) RT tensile elongation does not increase by at least 2% absolute compared to baseline; (2) 1600 °C strength decreases by more than 10% or creep rate increases by more than 20% at equal stress; (3) at 30 keV He to 1e18 He/m^2 and 500 °C, either bubble number density or average bubble radius is not reduced by at least 30%, or blistered area does not decrease by at least 30%; (4) irradiation or thermal exposure produces detectable second-phase precipitation (e.g., sigma/Laves or borides) exceeding 1 vol.%.
